title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking & runbooks
author: Sofia Ramirez
body:
Overview
========
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, the benchmarking suite, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical starting point for engineers working on runtime performance, capacity planning, and incident response.

Audience and ownership
----------------------
- Primary audience: Serving runtime engineers, SREs, perf engineers, and platform product owners.
- Owners: serving-runtime team (pager: #serving-runtime-oncall).
- Escalation: see the \"Oncall and incident response\" playbook for escalation matrix.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)
--------------------------------
Short intro
: The runtime is a modular, GPU-first inference engine plus an orchestration layer. Goals: low tail latencies (p50/p95 targets), predictable throughput, and graceful degradation across model families and hardware.

Key components
- Frontend API: validates requests, enforces quotas and auth, and provides request metadata (model, max_tokens, temperature, routing hints).
- Router: policy-driven routing (latency, cost, locality, customer tier) with fallback to compatible model shards/variants.
- Inference workers: GPU-backed processes that host model shards, manage KV cache, and run optimized kernels.
- Batcher: continuous batching layer that groups compatible requests and dispatches to workers while respecting latency SLOs.
- Cache layer: prefix and KV cache with sharding. Cache-aware batching reduces token compute for repeated prefixes.
- Telemetry & tracing: per-request tracing (span per component), token-level cost attribution, and heatmaps for kernel hotpaths.

SLOs and targets (serving-runtime core)
- Production p50 latency (text-gen, single-stream): < 60 ms for 128-token sequences on dedicated P4d-equivalent nodes.
- Production p95 latency: < 200 ms for 128-token sequences on dedicated nodes (goal).
- Token throughput per GPU varies by model family & quantization: see benchmarking table below.
- Availability: 99.95% for Hosted routes; Dedicated SLAs referenced in pricing docs.

2) Kernel scheduling design
--------------------------
Principles
1. Locality: keep KV cache and tensors local to a process to avoid cross-host transfers.
2. Adaptivity: choose kernel variants by sequence length and current occupancy (short-vs-long kernels).
3. Latency-first for low-tier customer traffic; throughput-first for batch/off-peak workloads where configured.

Scheduler components
- Short-request fast-path scheduler: picks minimized-latency kernels (fused attention / reduced launch overhead) for requests with seq_len <= 256.
- Long-request scheduler: picks numerically-stable kernels with memory-optimized tiling for seq_len > 256.
- Hybrid preemption: supports preempting batch work for high-priority single-stream requests when preemption budget allows.
- Kernel selector: runtime component that selects kernel implementation based on (model_type, seq_len, dtype, device_memory_pressure, quantization_profile).

Config knobs (config table)
| key | description | default | recommended range | owner |
| ---- | ----------- | ------- | ----------------- | ----- |
| scheduler.preemption_budget | max ms per-second allocated to preempt batches | "50" | "0-200" | Serving-runtime |
| scheduler.fast_path_seq_threshold | seq_len boundary for fast-path kernels | "256" | "64-512" | Serving-runtime |
| kernel_selector.fallback_timeout_ms | time to wait before falling back to slower kernel | "40" | "10-200" | Serving-runtime |

Operational notes
- When GPU memory pressure > 85% the kernel selector prefers memory-optimized kernels even if they are slightly slower. This prevents OOMs during rollouts.
- Kernel driver versions are pinned per release; see Release Notes -> Driver matrix.

3) Profiling playbook (how to reproduce, analyze, and act)
----------------------------------------------------------
Goals
- Identify hot kernels, memory pressure, NVLink/PCIe hotspots, and CPU-side serialization.
- Produce reproducible perf regression artifacts for CI and release reviews.

Quick checklist
1. Reproduce workload with the benchmarking harness (section 4). Use same model, tokenization, and input distribution.
2. Collect traces: enable verbose tracing for 30s of representative traffic. Commands: 
```
# enable trace sampling (example)
redwood-runtimectl trace enable --scope=worker-123 --duration=30s --rate=1.0
redwood-runtimectl profile gpu --device=0 --duration=30s --output=/tmp/prof-$(date +%s).nvtx
```
3. Capture kernel-level metrics: use ncu/nvprof or GPU vendor tools per pinned driver.
4. Capture CPU flame graphs (perf / py-spy) to find scheduling or marshalling bottlenecks.
5. Aggregate telemetry in the perf dashboard and open a perf issue with the collected artifacts.

Common symptoms & checks
- Symptom: sudden p95 spike when a new model version rolled out.
  - Check: kernel selector fallback logs; look for frequent kernel fallback events and increased launch times.
- Symptom: increased tail latency under steady load.
  - Check: batch sizes, scheduler.preemption_budget, and GC/paging on host.
- Symptom: OOM or CUDA out-of-memory on rollout.
  - Check: quantization profile mismatch, driver mismatch, recent model changes (longer max_seq_length).

Actionable mitigations
- Increase scheduler.preemption_budget to 100 ms if single-stream requests are starving; monitor throughput regressions.
- Pin the model to an earlier quantization profile and re-run the benchmark harness to validate.
- Roll back the kernel driver to the last-known-good version documented in the release notes.

4) Benchmarking suite (harness & metrics)
----------------------------------------
Overview
- The benchmarking suite (benchit) runs on a dedicated perf fleet and supports model families, quantization profiles, and sequence-length distributions. Outputs: throughput curves, latency histograms, kernel hotpath heatmaps, and cost-per-token estimates.

How to run (examples)
1. Smoke run locally:
```
benchit run --model redwood-open-7b --quant=8bit --seq-dist=wiki-avg --concurrency=32 --duration=120 --out=/tmp/bench.json
```
2. Full perf run on perf cluster (use perf account):
```
benchit run --cluster perf-us-east-1 --model family/X --quant=8bit --seq-dist=web-large --duration=3600 --concurrency=auto --out=s3://perf-artifacts/bench-$(date +%F).json
```
Key metrics collected
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms) per sequence length bucket
- tokens/sec per-GPU and aggregate tokens/sec
- kernel-level time breakdown (attention, matmul, softmax)
- cost-per-token estimate (based on pre-configured cloud pricing)

Benchmarking best practices
- Use production-like token distributions; synthetic short-only workloads give misleading kernel choices.
- Include both cold-start and warm-KV-cache runs.
- For model rollouts, run canary bench with the canary traffic mix and compare diffs to control.

5) Release notes (runtime-specific highlights)
--------------------------------------------
Summary of recent changes (2029-05 -> 2029-06 release)
- Kernel selector v3.2: improved latency for short sequences by ~12% on A100 and P4-class instances.
- Hybrid preemption: enabled by default for Hosted tier; preemption budget default set to 50ms.
- Benchit: added cost-per-token module and sequence-distribution presets for common workloads.
- Fixed: race condition in KV cache invalidation that could cause stale-prefix hits during model version swaps.
- Driver matrix: pinned CUDA 13.2 + vendor hotfix 13.2.1 for A100 and H100 families.

Upgrade checklist for runtime maintainers
1. Run benchit against representative models and confirm no >5% regressions for p95.
2. Validate driver versions on staging fleet.
3. Coordinate rollout with infra to ensure capacity headroom.

6) Known issues (current)
------------------------
- ISSUE-2029-112: Intermittent kernel fallback loops with mixed-precision models when sequence-length boundaries oscillate rapidly. Workaround: set scheduler.fast_path_seq_threshold to a lower bound (200) for affected routes. Status: in_review.
- ISSUE-2029-121: Under very high small-request load (<= 16 tokens) p99 latency can spike due to syscall overhead. Workaround: enable batching-aside small_request_burst throttle. Status: published (mitigation available).
- ISSUE-2029-134: Rare OOM on H100 with large prompt concatenations when KV cache replication triggers. Workaround: lower cache replication factor to 1 for affected clusters. Status: draft.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)
-------------------------------------------
Runbook: High p95 latency on Hosted route
- Pager: #serving-runtime-oncall.
- Steps:
  1. Check route-specific dashboards (latency, error rate, request volume).
  2. Run a targeted benchit smoke run using the same model + seq-dist.
  3. Check kernel selector logs: 
     - grep \"kernel_fallback\" /var/log/serving/runtime/worker-*/kernel.log
  4. If fallback events predominating, increase kernel_selector.fallback_timeout_ms to 80 ms and retest.
  5. If OOMs are observed, scale up the node pool or pin model to a smaller quantization profile.
  6. If issue persists, open an incident and attach perf artifacts: benchit outputs, nvprof traces, and runtime traces.

Runbook: OOM during rollout
- Steps:
  1. Pause rollout and mark affected nodes as drain-only.
  2. Check recent model commit for increased max_seq_length or new operators.
  3. Compare quantization_profile in release bundle against last-known-good.
  4. If driver mismatch suspected, roll back driver on one staging node and reproduce.
  5. If immediate mitigation required: reduce autoscale target and revert to previous model version.

- Benchit repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/benchit (README includes sequence-distribution presets).

Appendix A: Example diagnostic commands
-------------------------------------
- Trace enable (ctl): redwood-runtimectl trace enable --scope=worker-123 --duration=30s --rate=1.0
- Local benchit quick run: benchit run --model redwood-open-7b --quant=8bit --concurrency=16 --duration=120
- Fetch kernel logs: sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime-worker --since \"15 minutes ago\" | grep -i kernel
